A top-down shooter with a black-and-white hand-drawn art style, set against the backdrop of late 19th-century American cowboy culture. Unfortunately, the experience is far from enjoyable. The game still suffers from numerous severe bugs that remain officially unfixed, heavily damaging the overall experience. On top of that, the story is nothing remarkable—starting with some promise but ultimately fizzling out. Much of the writing, narrative delivery, and character dialogue feels painfully mediocre, if not outright poor.

What genuinely puzzles me is why this game has such a high positive rating. Interestingly, only [b] 13.4% of players have unlocked the completion achievement [/b]. In other words, out of everyone who owns this game, only 13.4% were willing to actually finish it.

From a gameplay standpoint, there are many frustrating design issues. Enemy placement often feels unreasonable, to the point where enemies can shoot and kill you from outside your limited field of vision before you even have a chance to see them. The enemy aggro system also seems bugged. Sometimes, you can quietly sneak past enemies without making a sound or even entering their line of sight, only for one of them to suddenly spin around and instantly gun you down. Other times, you can fire your weapon right in front of a sleeping enemy and they remain peacefully asleep as if trapped in eternal slumber.

What hurts the game most is its overwhelming sense of repetition. The monotonous visual style, simplistic gunplay, and recycled level design all pile together into an experience that becomes genuinely tedious and exhausting—especially in the mid-to-late game, where it starts to feel like a chore to push through.

Ironically, the black-and-white sketchbook aesthetic becomes part of the problem at that point. Combined with the frustration that naturally builds up over time, the visual monotony makes it harder to distinguish enemies, doors, breakable windows, and solid walls. Rather than enhancing immersion, the art style ends up hurting the overall gameplay flow.

Most importantly, I have to strongly warn people about the game's severe bugs, many of which have also been reported by other players in their reviews. For example, the game may randomly crash in Chapter 2, which can directly corrupt your save file. Even simply quitting and relaunching the game can sometimes reset all your money and collectibles (such as hats) back to zero, forcing you to painfully collect everything again—and unfortunately, I personally ran into this issue. Some players have also reported outright save corruption without even crashing; they simply exited the game and came back to find their save broken. All I can really do is wish you good luck and hope you don't run into these problems yourself.

All things considered, I cannot recommend this game. The overall experience is simply too rough. If I had to recommend it to anyone, it would only be to players looking to casually kill time, or those who are particularly interested in this setting and gameplay style. If you're not expecting a deep experience—or even a full playthrough—and just want something to casually mess around with during downtime for the atmosphere and theme, then this game [i] might [/i] still be worth considering.

12 is Better Than 6 is a really fun top-down shooter that reminded me a lot of Hotline Miami.

You shoot your way through enemies while progressing through the story. I really enjoyed the ability to change hats, pick different perks, and choose from various weapons. Experimenting with different weapon and perk combinations was fun, and collecting all the hats was surprisingly enjoyable. Getting the achievement for having them all felt very satisfying.

For achievement hunters there are some challenging tasks, but the difficulty is set just right. I also loved the unique pen and ink art style.

Overall the game was enjoyable from start to finish, mixing solid action with light strategy and planning.

Definitely recommend if you like top-down shooters with a simple story and some room for experimentation.

Recommended: Fun top-down shooter with cool art style, weapon variety, perks, hat collecting, and satisfying achievements.

12 is Better Than 6 est une vraie bonne surprise.
Pour son prix, la durée de vie est plus que correcte, et le jeu va droit au but.
Pas de remplissage inutile, juste une progression efficace et un rythme qui tient jusqu’à la fin.

Le gameplay façon Hotline Miami reste original et rafraîchissant.
C’est nerveux, précis, et chaque erreur se paie immédiatement.
La patte graphique en style dessin au crayon donne une vraie identité au jeu.
Ce n’est pas juste un choix esthétique, ça apporte une âme, une ambiance unique qu’on reconnaît instantanément.

La courbe de difficulté est globalement bien dosée.
Rien d’injuste, mais quelques passages plus exigeants sur la fin qui demandent un peu plus de concentration.
C’est léger, mais suffisant pour garder l’attention et éviter la routine.

Là où ça coince vraiment, c’est du côté des succès.
“Le Maître des chapeaux” est franchement pénible : sans tuto, il faut quasiment revisiter chaque niveau pour ne rien rater.
Ça casse le rythme et oblige à jouer de manière artificielle.
Et “Quoi ? Y’a une histoire ?” est encore plus maladroit : devoir passer plusieurs dialogues pour le débloquer complique la compréhension du scénario.
Soit tu recommences certaines missions, soit tu fais comme moi et tu passes tout… au risque de passer totalement à côté de l’histoire.
C’est dommage, parce que ça va à l’encontre de l’expérience naturelle du jeu.

Malgré ces défauts, le titre reste court, impactant, reconnaissable et efficace.
Il était presque parfait à mes yeux.
Je le recommande quand même sans hésiter, et j’ai passé un vrai bon moment à décrocher le 100%.
